1:
The chapter opens without a break. grammatical-historical Ellicott calls the division of chapters unfortunate, since Let not your heart be troubled answers directly to what has just been said — the traitor indicated, the departure announced, Peter’s denial foretold. Robertson, of the same school, notes that the heart here is not the physical organ but the seat of the spiritual life, the centre of feeling and faith; the disciples’ hearts were tossed like waves in the wind. Lightfoot presses the particular grief: they had run along with their whole nation in expecting the kingdom restored to Israel through the Messiah, and had got little by following him but poverty, contempt and reproach. Barnes sets the words at the table during the supper and calls the three chapters that follow the consolatory part of the faith, fitted to allay every fear and silence every murmur.

reformed Gill lists the causes: the loss of Christ’s bodily presence, the betrayal by one of them and the denial by another, the collapse of the hope of a temporal kingdom, and the persecutions ahead. Calvin looks past the causes to the remedy. Christ does not simply exhort them to be steadfast, but tells them where courage is to be had — by faith, when he is acknowledged to be the Son of God, who has in himself a sufficiency of strength for maintaining the safety of his followers. Calvin insists we attend to when the words were spoken: a contest was at hand in which they would see him on a cross, a spectacle offering nothing but ground for the lowest despair.

The latin-fathers rest the comfort on Christ’s divinity. Augustine of Hippo puts it as an inference: it follows as a consequence that if they believe in God they ought to believe also in him, which were no consequence if Christ were not God. The same voice adds that he emptied himself not by losing the form of God but by taking the form of a servant. Augustine, in the catena, draws the line and then turns it pastoral: you are in fear for this form of a servant — let not your heart be troubled, the form of God shall raise it up.

The witnesses divide on a point of grammar with consequences. grammatical-historical Ellicott takes both clauses as imperatives, Believe in God, believe also in me, holding there is no good reason for the English version’s mixed reading, the present trouble arising from a want of true belief in God. Robertson agrees the two Greek forms are identical and that both are probably imperatives — keep on believing. reformed Calvin allows the imperative but prefers the received reading, and is struck that faith in the Father should be named first at all, since Christ is the lively image of the Father. His answer is that all assent to belief in God as an admitted principle, yet scarce one in a hundred actually believes it, God’s naked majesty standing at too great a distance; so the Son holds himself out as the object faith may rest on. puritan-evangelical Henry gives both readings and leans to the second, taking the first clause as acknowledgement and the second as the command they still needed.

Henry also weighs where the stress falls: on troubled, be not put into hurry and confusion; on heart, the main fort, to be kept when nothing else can be kept; on your, since disciples should keep their minds quiet when everything else is unquiet. wesleyan-arminian Clarke reads the words as addressed to the disciples immediately after Peter was answered, telling them not to be afflicted at his leaving nor to lose courage at what had been said of the denial. Wesley compresses the whole: the trouble is at his departure, and the believing is the sum of all this discourse, urged until they did believe.
2:
reformed Gill takes the Father’s house to be heaven, named to draw their minds off an earthly kingdom; the mansions are abiding places of love, peace, joy and rest, and many denotes fulness and sufficiency of room for all his people. Calvin agrees that Christ is removing the suspicion that he will ascend and leave them on earth without further notice: he goes before, not to dwell in heaven in a private capacity, but that it might be the common inheritance of all the godly. Calvin then faces the question this forces — what was the condition of the fathers after death, before Christ ascended? — and answers that they were not shut in a prison but set as on a watch-tower, looking for the promised redemption, and now enjoy a blessed rest.

grammatical-historical Ellicott works from the words. The Greek for mansions recurs in the New Testament only at v.23, where it is rendered abode; Wiclif and the Geneva version read dwellings, and the translators here followed the Vulgate’s mansiones, which in Elizabethan English meant nothing grander than a resting-place. The point is the extent of the Father’s house: no risk of its being overcrowded like the caravanserai at Bethlehem, or the lodgings in which the Passover pilgrims were then sheltering at Jerusalem. Robertson calls this the most precious picture of heaven we possess, the heavenly home with the Father and with Jesus, and notes that if it were not so leaves its verb unexpressed, a condition determined as unfulfilled. Lightfoot sets the promise beside the ark of the covenant going before Israel to search out a resting place (Numbers 10:33), a parallel Clarke adopts from him and Robertson echoes as the custom of sending one forward.

Whether many implies grades of blessedness is the sharpest division. wesleyan-arminian Clarke reads it plainly as various degrees of glory, suited to the various capacities and attainments of Christ’s followers, and finds the image in the chambers within the temple precincts. Gill denies it outright: the saints are all loved with the same love, bought with the same price, justified with the same righteousness and equally the sons of God, so their glory will be the same. Calvin calls the degrees reading an error — the mansions are not said to be different or unlike, only enough for a great number. Ellicott takes a middle line, that happiness depends on the mind which receives it and must therefore vary, but that this is not the prominent thought here. Wesley simply counts the room: enough for the holy angels, for their predecessors in the faith, for all who now believe, and for a great multitude no one can number.

Barnes offers a reading he says has not occurred to interpreters — that the Father’s house may include the whole universe, the earth one mansion and heaven another, so that dying is only a removal from one apartment of God’s vast dwelling-place to another. He and Ellicott both hear if it were not so, I would have told you as an appeal to Christ’s candour: no truth concealed, no ill-founded hope left to be cherished. Clarke turns it the same way: he would not have permitted them a vain hope. Calvin instead supplies the suppressed clause — had the heavenly glory awaited him only, he would have told them there was no room for any but himself. On I will come again, Ellicott presses the present tense, I am coming again, and refers it to his constant spiritual presence, the reception to himself being the complete union that presence begins. Robertson and Calvin read it instead of the last day, Robertson adding that for believers who die first the promise is fulfilled in their death.
4:
The saying looks backward and forward at once, and the witnesses divide over how much the disciples really possessed. puritan-evangelical Henry hears two senses in ye know. First, you may know: this is none of the secret things that belong not to you, but one of the things revealed — you need not ascend into heaven nor go down into the deep, for the word is near you, level to you. Second, you do know: you know that which is the home and that which is the way, though perhaps not as the home and as the way. Henry draws a pastoral rule from it — Christ is willing to make the best of his people’s knowledge, weak and defective as it is, and knows the good in them better than they know it themselves, being certain they have a knowledge, faith and love of which they are not themselves sensible.

reformed Gill grants only the minimum: they might have known at least where he was going, since he had spoken of his Father’s house and of preparing a place there, and doubtless had some knowledge of it, though very confused and imperfect. grammatical-historical Barnes is firmer — he had so often told them he was to die, and rise, and ascend, that they could not but understand it; and the way they were to tread was to obey his precepts, imitate his example, and follow him. Clarke, of the wesleyan-arminian line, says the same in a sentence: he had told them so often and so plainly that they must certainly have comprehended it. Robertson reads the clause as a definite allusion to the puzzle that had stopped Peter a few verses earlier, and says simply that the path to the Father’s house is now plain.

Ellicott presses the text itself. The better reading, he argues, joins the clauses — and whither I go, ye know the way — that is, you know that I am the way to the Father, where I am going. They did not indeed fully know this, but the means of knowing lay within their reach and his own words had declared it. They ought to have known it, and the saying is meant to set what they ought to have known against what they actually did know, so that he may instruct them the more fully. To know our ignorance, Ellicott adds, is the first step to its removal.

Calvin takes the verse as a second consolation laid on the first. The point is that Christ’s death is not a destruction but a passage to the Father, and that the disciples must travel the same road if they are to share the same glory. Both clauses, he insists, deserve care: we must first see Christ by the eyes of faith in the heavenly glory and a blessed immortality, and then know that he is the first-fruits of our life, and that what was closed against us has been opened by him. Wesley compresses the second clause to three words — the way is of faith, holiness, sufferings.

Among the latin-fathers, Augustine of Hippo reads the earlier words by the later. The mansions of which Christ said both that they already were in his Father’s house and that he was going to prepare them exist already in predestination, and are also being prepared by the purifying through faith of the hearts of those who are afterwards to inhabit them — for those hearts are themselves the house of God. To dwell in God’s house is nothing else than to be numbered among his people, his people being at once in God and God in them. The departure is itself the preparing: by believing in him though he is no longer visible, the mansion whose outward form stays hidden in the future is being made ready now.
5:
eastern-antiochene Chrysostom notes that if the Jews who wished to be rid of Christ asked where he was going, much more the disciples, who wished never to be separated from him; they ask with love and fear together. grammatical-historical Ellicott notes that the Lord laid the stress on the way and Thomas lays it on the whither: his mind seeks measured certainty, and without the destination he cannot think about the road. Robertson points out that it is Thomas, not Peter, who renews the doubt, and calls him spokesman for the materialistic conception then and now. reformed Gill says he betrays his ignorance here as elsewhere his unbelief, and speaks for the rest by judging them from himself. Barnes blames prejudice: they still held the common notions of a temporal kingdom, and had Thomas laid aside those opinions and received the truth as plainly spoken, faith would have been easy and natural. Calvin refuses to read the reply as contradiction: Thomas did not mean to give his Master the lie, but the knowledge of the saints is sometimes confused, since they do not grasp the manner or reason of things certain and already explained — and before setting out we must know where we mean to go.

The latin-fathers answer that they knew the way because they knew him. Augustine glosses it clause by clause: I am the way, whereby you would go; the truth, whereto you would go; the life, in which you would abide. Everyone understands the truth and the life, but not everyone has found the way; the Word, who is truth and life with the Father, by taking human nature is made the way. Walk by the Man and you will arrive at God; better to limp on the right road than walk stoutly on the wrong.

reformed Calvin hears three degrees — beginning, middle and end — so that we begin with Christ, continue in him and end in him; whoever is not satisfied with him alone strives after something beyond absolute perfection. He also notes that Christ declines the question asked, checking curiosity about his condition in heaven to press the more necessary matter of how we become partakers of the blessed resurrection. wesleyan-arminian Wesley distributes the titles instead: to the question about the way, I am the way; about knowledge, the truth; about whither, the life. Clarke gives four ways in which Christ is the way: doctrine, example, sacrifice, Spirit.

Lightfoot asks why truth and life are added when the question concerned only the way, and gives two answers: a Hebrew idiom by which the phrase means the true and living way, and a refutation of the Jewish estimate of the law as being itself way, truth and life. Cyril of Jerusalem presses the exclusive clause against those who think to be made friends of the Father apart from devotion toward the Son: he who refuses the Way and denies the Door, how shall he be deemed worthy of entrance? Ellicott makes the pronoun emphatic — I, and none besides me — and adds that the true whither is a state now and hereafter rather than a place far above. Robertson says there is no use wincing at the words: if he is the incarnate Son of God they are necessarily true.

Gill guards the first title: Christ is not the way merely as an example going before, nor as a prophet pointing it out, but the way of salvation itself by his obedience and sacrifice. Barnes says the Jewish ceremonies were shadows and the life of Jesus the truth. eastern-alexandrian Origen counts rather than expounds: the Son is announced under a plurality of names of good things — life, light, truth, the way that leads to the truth, the resurrection, the door — and by numbering them we learn how many good things he is.
7:
grammatical-historical Ellicott insists the emphasis of the first clause falls not on me but on known, and that the better text uses two different Greek verbs, one for knowing by observation and the other by reflection. Rendered exactly: if you had recognised who I really am, you would have known that I and my Father are one. Robertson makes the point from the other end: the first verb is a past perfect of the word for knowing by personal experience, in a second-class condition, so that Thomas and the rest had not really come to know Jesus, much as they loved him. The second clause he reads as inchoative, ye are beginning to know the Father from now on. Because they had seen the image of God, God is like Jesus Christ — a bold and daring claim to deity, and the only intelligible conception of God there is.

The reformed witnesses locate the deficiency elsewhere. Gill will not have it that they were ignorant: they knew Christ to be the Son of God, the Saviour of the world and true Messiah, but were not yet so thoroughly acquainted with his person, power and office. Calvin makes the failure a failure of acknowledgement. It is foolish and pernicious curiosity, he says, when men not satisfied with Christ try to reach God by indirect and crooked paths; they grant that nothing is better than the knowledge of God, yet when he is near and speaks familiarly they wander through their own speculations and seek above the clouds the one they will not own as present. The reproof is that the disciples had not yet acknowledged the lively image of the Father exhibited in Christ — and the saying was framed rather to commend the doctrine than to extol their faith, charging them with ingratitude if they will not consider what has been given them.

Barnes agrees they were truly disciples and lacked only a full and accurate knowledge of Christ’s character and designs, still retaining the Jewish notions of a temporal Messiah. A correct knowledge of the work of Christ, he concludes, simply is a correct knowledge of the counsels of God, and what blocks it is prejudice. Lightfoot supplies the history behind that prejudice: it was hard enough to spell the Messiah out of the law and the prophets under the first temple, when Moses had only his own veil and the prophets their own obscurity, but under the second the obscurity was doubled by the darkness and smoke of traditions, which brought in doctrines diametrically contrary to the chief articles of faith. The apostles did own Jesus as Messiah; if they judged amiss about his office, that must be set to the account of an epidemic distemper of the whole nation which they still in some measure laboured under. wesleyan-arminian Clarke offers two grounds at once: because Christ and the Father are one, and because a proper examination of the intention and design of the law would have convinced them that it referred to him.

Among the latin-fathers, Augustine of Hippo begins from a rule of reading — the words of the Gospel are rightly understood only when found to agree with those before them, since the premises ought to agree with the conclusion when it is the Truth that speaks. Applying it, he presses the earlier promise: if they are to be where he is, where else but in himself? He is himself that eternal life which is yet to be theirs; and as the Father has life in himself, so has he given the Son to have life in himself, the Son being the very life he possesses.
8:
grammatical-historical Ellicott says Philip catches at the word seen and thinks of some revelation of the glory of God such as was granted to Moses, or of the vision three of their number were given on the mountain; one such sight of the Father, he supposes, would end every doubt and satisfy their deepest longing. Clarke, of the wesleyan-arminian line, notes the same parallel with Moses and adds an excuse: in Peter, James or John the request would have been inexcusable, but Philip had not been on the mount of transfiguration, and since Christ was introducing a new law he wished a fresh manifestation with it. Lightfoot puts the thought into Philip’s own mouth — when the law was given to Moses the Israelites saw God in his glory; now that a new law and economy is being brought in, show us the Father and his glory, and we shall doubt no more. Robertson agrees Philip was possibly hoping for a theophany, and certainly had not grasped what Jesus had just said. Barnes concedes it was right to want evidence that Jesus was the Messiah, but says such evidence had already been afforded abundantly in the miracles and the teaching, and should have sufficed.

The Greek and Latin witnesses read the request differently. latin-fathers Hilary holds that Philip did not deny the Father could be seen, but wished to be shown him — not with the bodily eye, but so that the one he had already seen might be made manifest to his understanding. He had seen the Son in the form of man; how through that form he saw the Father he did not know, and that is what he asks to have shown. Hilary then turns the reproof on him: the works had been strictly divine — walking on the water, commanding the winds, remitting sins, raising the dead — and the complaint is that in the humanity Christ had assumed the divine nature was still not discerned. eastern-antiochene John Chrysostom takes the opposite view of what Philip wanted, holding that he desired to see with these bodily eyes, having perhaps heard that the prophets saw God — but those, he answers, were acts of condescension, since no one has seen God at any time and no one shall see his face and live.

John Chrysostom also explains the timing. Peter and the Jews had asked who the Father was, and Thomas had asked, and no one had learnt anything clear; so Philip, not wishing to seem importunate by asking in his turn, softened the request with and it sufficeth us — we seek no more. But he reversed the order. Christ had said that knowing him was the way to knowing the Father, and Philip asks for the Father as though he already knew Christ exactly. Christ will not endure that, but puts him in the right way, persuading him to come at the knowledge of the Father through himself; and the reproof is pointed, for he does not say hast thou not seen me but hast thou not known me. From this very closeness, he warns, some have run to the opposite error of collapsing the Father and the Son into one person, which the wording is framed to exclude.

reformed Gill notes only that Philip addresses Christ reverently, as Thomas had, speaks in the name of them all, and in asking owns their ignorance of the Father. Calvin turns the episode outward. It seems very absurd, he grants, that the apostles should keep raising objections to the Lord, since he had spoken precisely to inform them on the point in question — yet there is not one of the faults described here that may not be charged on us as well as on them. We profess to be in earnest in seeking God; and when he presents himself before our eyes, we are blind.
9:
grammatical-historical Ellicott renders the question more exactly as hast thou not recognised me, matching the verb used two verses earlier, and hears in it a note of sadness and of warning — the loneliness of a holiness and greatness that is not understood. The close of the life is at hand, and Philip, who had followed from the first, shows by his question that he never learned what the work and purpose of that life had been. The warning, he adds, speaks to all Christian teachers: it is possible to stand in the closest apparent nearness to Christ and never learn the meaning of the words one constantly hears and utters. Robertson notes the emphatic thou — after these years together — and says Jesus patiently repeats himself in a crisp statement. Barnes fills in the interval: for more than three years he had been with them, raising the dead, casting out devils, healing the sick, doing what no one could do who had not come from God, so that they had full opportunity to learn his character and mission; after such proofs no visible manifestation was needed. reformed Gill lists the same: familiar conversation, teaching, and miracles over so long a time.

Barnes takes care over what kind of seeing is meant: hath seen me means has seen the works, heard the doctrines and understood the character, having given proper attention to the proofs of a divine mission; and that the Father here denotes the divine nature, God regarded as Father, rather than the distinction of persons. It cannot refer to the essence or substance of God, which is invisible; all that is meant by God being seen is that some manifestation has been made from which his character may be learned. Calvin puts the failure back on Philip: he had God present in Christ and did not behold him, prevented by nothing but his own ingratitude. Those hurried into speculation because Christ alone does not satisfy them make little progress; the desire springs from the meanness of his low condition, which is unreasonable, since by that humiliation he exhibits the infinite goodness of God.

wesleyan-arminian Clarke asks whether any creature could say these words, and whether they do not evidently imply that Christ declared himself the everlasting God. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem builds the claim out carefully. In all things the Son is like him who begat him, begotten Life of Life and Light of Light, Power of Power, God of God, and the characteristics of the Godhead are unchangeable in the Son, so that whoever is counted worthy to behold Godhead in the Son attains the fruition of the Father. He then guards it on both sides: neither separate them nor confuse them, neither call the Son foreign to the Father nor allow those who make the Father sometimes Father and sometimes Son. Having begotten the Son the Father remained the Father, unchanged: he begat Wisdom yet lost no wisdom, begat Power yet became not weak, begat God yet lost not his own Godhead.

Ellicott closes by making the exchange perennial. Philip’s demand is constantly repeated — give us something in religion on which the soul can rest; we are weary of the doubts and strifes and dogmas too often called religion; give us truth, give us life, and we will gladly embrace it. All of that, he answers, is the heart of the child seeking the presence of the Father, and that Father has been manifested in the person of the Son, in whom is the full revelation of God and bread enough for every want of every man. He that has seen him has seen the Father: how then can men still say, show us the Father?
10:
grammatical-historical Ellicott notes that the order of the clauses is reversed from the earlier statement of this truth, in keeping with a context about knowing the Son and knowing the Father through him. He argues that the words that I speak covers not the present teaching chiefly but the whole manifestation of the character and attributes of God: all Christ’s words had been a revelation of the Father whom Philip now asks to see. He prefers the better reading of the second clause, that the Father who dwells in him doeth his own works, and takes both together as the proof of the mutual indwelling. Barnes fixes on the wording: the Father remaining in me denotes a union more intimate than can subsist between a mere man and God, for a mere prophet would have said that the Father who commissioned him does the works. Robertson observes that Jesus had a right to expect greater faith from these men than from the blind man or Martha.

reformed Calvin refuses to read the verse first as metaphysics: the words refer not to Christ’s divine essence but to the manner of the revelation; Christ is not asking what he is in himself but what we ought to acknowledge him to be, so the description applies to his power rather than his essence. He at once grants that the ancient writers take no erroneous view in quoting the passage for Christ’s divinity: full divinity dwells in him and displays its power. Calvin then meets an objection: might not the prophets be called sons of God on the same ground, having spoken by inspiration? The answer lies in what the doctrine contains — the prophets send their disciples to another, while Christ attaches them to himself. wesleyan-arminian Clarke and Wesley put it flatly: Father and Son are one in essence and one in operation, and such miracles could be wrought only by unlimited power. Gill notes that some copies, with the Vulgate, read the clause as a question — believe ye not?

Among the latin-fathers, Augustine of Hippo begins by asking whether the words are themselves works, and answers that they are, since whoever edifies a neighbour by what he says works a good work. He reads I speak not of myself as meaning: I who speak am not of myself — Christ attributing what he does to the one of whom he is. The Father is God, but not God of anyone else, and Light, but not of light; the Son is God of God and Light of Light, equal to the Father yet born of him. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem guards the formula by its exact wording: he does not say I am the Father but the Father is in me, and I am in the Father, so that we neither separate nor confuse them. They are one in the dignity belonging to Godhead, since God begat God, and one in kingdom.

The second verse offers a fallback. Ellicott sees Christ passing from Philip to the whole body of the apostles, claiming a personal trust that would accept his statement outright; if they cannot receive it on the testimony of his word he takes lower ground and sets before them the evidence he had offered the Jews. Barnes counts two grounds — his own testimony, or else his works — either of which should have sufficed. Robertson calls it a repeated appeal, the imperative used at the opening of the chapter. Gill puts the alternative in Christ’s voice: take my word for it, or else believe for the sake of the doctrines preached to you, such as no mere man ever spoke or delivered with such authority. Wesley refines the appeal to works: what is meant is not the miracles themselves but the sovereign, Godlike way of performing them.
12:
Two questions govern the verse: who is promised this, and how the works are greater. reformed Gill is restrictive — the words are not to be understood of every private believer, but only of the apostles. grammatical-historical Barnes agrees it had peculiar reference to the apostles, consoling men full of grief with the honour awaiting them; it cannot cover all his followers, since not all Christians have possessed power to do greater works. eastern-antiochene Chrysostom presses the wider wording: these works Christ did through his apostles, yet he includes others besides them when he says he that believeth in me. The apparent harshness — are we to count no one a believer who does not do greater works? — he answers by the apostolic word that faith is counted for righteousness to him who believes in the one who justifies the ungodly; by that work, the very believing, the works of Christ are done. Ellicott takes the same broad line, finding the fulfilment not in instances of apostolic power but in the whole work of the Church.

Barnes denies that greater can refer to the miracles themselves, since no higher exertion of power is possible than raising the dead; they were greater in effect, making a deeper impression and converting more sinners, whereas the works of Jesus were confined to Judea and seen by few. Robertson says it in a phrase: not greater miracles, nor greater in quality, but greater in quantity. Chrysostom reaches a similar place by another road, holding that by works Christ refers to his words, whose fruit was faith; the converts made by his own speaking were few beside those the disciples made by preaching, so that he did greater works when preached by the believing than when speaking in men’s ears.

wesleyan-arminian Clarke lists what was done — a shadow that healed the diseased, handkerchiefs carried from an apostle’s body, two liars struck dead at a word, a sorcerer struck blind — and adds that Christ preached in Judea only and in that country’s language, while the apostles preached through most of the known world. But he ranks the moral miracle highest: it is the greatest miracle of divine grace to convert the obstinate heart of man from sin to holiness. Wesley gives the same catalogue and verdict — converting one sinner is a greater work than all these — and reads the closing clause as the reason: he goes to the Father to send the Holy Ghost.

puritan-evangelical Henry sets the promise against the disciples’ fear of being left as sheep without a shepherd. They are to be clothed with power sufficient to bear them out, and more ample power than when first sent out. This does not weaken the argument from Christ’s works but strengthens it, since the apostles’ miracles were wrought in his name and by faith in him; nothing magnifies his power more than that he gave others power to work them too. Calvin adds why the clause was needed: everything said so far, as it concerned them, was temporal, and our memory is short — when God has loaded us with every blessing, if he pauses a fortnight we fancy he is no longer alive. So Christ promises an uninterrupted conviction of his power for the future. The ascension was soon followed by a wonderful conversion of the world, in which his divinity was more powerfully displayed than while he dwelt among men.

Ellicott presses it furthest. He who becomes one with the Son by faith has the Son, and therefore the Father, dwelling in him, and becomes an instrument through which God carries his own works into effect. Pentecost was the first fulfilment, but so has been every revival of a truly religious spirit and every mission field; and in the world-wide extent of Christianity there is a work greater than any Christ did in the flesh.
13:
Everything here turns on the phrase in my name. grammatical-historical Barnes explains it as equivalent to saying on my account, and illustrates it: a son who authorises us to ask his father for aid because we are the son’s friends has us apply in the son’s name, and the favour comes from the regard the father bears his son. So we approach God in the name of his Son, and though undeserving are loved on his account. No privilege, he adds, is greater than approaching God in that name. Robertson calls this the first mention of the name as the open sesame to the Father’s will, and notes that although elsewhere the Father answers prayer, here and in the next verse the Son answers it himself.

Ellicott insists that both the width and the limitation of the promise be noted. It is whatsoever ye shall ask, and it is ask in my name — that is, as Christ’s representatives, doing his work, living in his spirit, seeking as he sought the Father’s will. It follows that merely personal petitions are not contemplated except so far as they are for the glory of God, and that petitions asked in ignorance may be most truly answered when they are not granted. The prayer in the garden — not my will but thine be done — should teach what prayer in his name and spirit means. We attach the words through Jesus Christ our Lord without bearing in mind that this implies an absolute self-sacrifice, and is itself a petition that our prayers not be answered except so far as they accord with the divine will.

The others draw the boundary differently. reformed Gill leaves it wide open: assistance in preaching, miraculous operations to confirm the gospel, its success, or any blessings whatsoever, for themselves or others. wesleyan-arminian Clarke reads it narrowly of the mission just promised, power to work miracles and convert souls; and by going to the Father, Christ will receive the Holy Spirit and send down his abundant influences. Barnes takes a middle position: it referred particularly to the apostles in spreading the gospel, yet holds for all Christians if what they ask is in faith and according to God’s will; and Christ can make it good, being exalted and possessed of all power.

Calvin makes the promise a statement about mediation. Christ declares that he will be the author of everything done by the apostles’ hands, and discharged the office of Mediator from the moment he entered the heavenly sanctuary. The end of all things is the hallowing of God’s name, and here its true method is declared: the majesty of God, hidden in itself, shines in Christ, so that in the benefits the Father bestows we have no right to separate the Son from him.

The repeated verse draws comment of its own. Gill reports that some think the words crept in from the margin, but takes them as repeated to strengthen the disciples’ faith. Ellicott calls it an emphatic repetition of both the width of the promise and its condition, with the stress now falling on the pronoun — I, on my part, will do it. Robertson notes that the reading ask me is supported by strong manuscripts and by the Latin and Syriac, that the phrase occurs nowhere else in this Gospel, and that if genuine, as he thinks likely, direct prayer to Jesus is here taught. Calvin calls the repetition anything but useless. All feel their unworthiness to approach God, yet most rush forward rashly; and afterwards, when the unworthiness returns to mind, each contrives expedients and passes through many windings rather than keep the road. By saying it a second time, Christ lays his hand on us, so that we may not lose our pains by fruitlessly seeking other intercessors.
15:
eastern-antiochene John Chrysostom notes the placement: after whatsoever ye shall ask, I will do it, lest they think mere asking availing, Christ adds if ye love me; and since they would be troubled at I go to the Father, he tells them that to be troubled now is not to love — to love is to obey. Everywhere, he says, we need works and not a show of words, for many profess to love God while their works show the contrary. Chrysostom adds that since they had longed for his bodily presence, he assures them his absence will be supplied another way. puritan-evangelical Henry takes the commandments for godliness in general and the apostolic trust in particular, and notes that Christ presses duty while comforting them, since comfort is to be expected only in the way of duty, and while they show love by grief, bidding them show it instead by conscientious care to perform their trust.

grammatical-historical Barnes holds that mere profession is no proof: the evidence a child loves its parents is willingness, without murmuring, to do all the parent requires. Robertson finds a condition of continuance, if ye keep on loving me, and prefers the future ye will keep to an imperative, since continued love prevents disobedience. Ellicott adds that my is emphatic: the commandments received from him, those of this last discourse chiefly. wesleyan-arminian Clarke says obedience will be received as a greater proof of affection than their tears; Wesley notes that immediately after faith comes the exhortation to love and good works. reformed Gill observes that Christ does not doubt their love but argues from it; Calvin grants it sincere yet mixed with superstition, since it was very foolish of them to wish to keep him in the world, and says the love we bear Christ is faulty if it is not directed to a pure obedience.

On the promise the dispute is largely over a word. Ellicott says the pronoun is again emphatic — I have given you your part, I on my part will pray — that the verb implies more nearness than the one rendered ask earlier, and that Comforter is better rendered Advocate, the word John elsewhere applies to Christ. Robertson explains it is another of like kind rather than a different sort, the term used of a legal pleader: Christ is our Paraclete with the Father, the Spirit the Father’s Paraclete with us. Clarke lets it carry its whole range — comforter, advocate, counsellor, patron, mediator — and divides the offices: Christ transacts our souls’ concerns with God, the Spirit the cause of God and Christ with us. Lightfoot resists the shift, since among the Messiah’s titles in Jewish writings Menahem, the Comforter, has chiefly obtained and his days are called the days of consolation; the promise answers that expectation.

Calvin resolves a tension: here the Spirit is the Father’s gift obtained by Christ’s prayer, while elsewhere Christ promises to send him — both correct, since as Mediator he obtains the grace and as God he bestows it. Gill likewise takes Christ to speak as Mediator; Barnes refers the praying to the intercession after the ascension, and calls the other Comforter a compensation for his absence. Wesley presses the another, Christ himself being one, and the for ever, which reaches to their followers in faith to the end of the world. latin-fathers Bede draws doctrine from the two titles: naming him the Spirit of truth shows he is Christ’s own, and saying the Father gives him declares him the Father’s also, so the Holy Ghost proceeds from both. Augustine of Hippo attends to the manner of the promise, warning that these few words hold more for inquiry than can be searched out. Cyril of Jerusalem gathers the titles, showing that Comforter, Holy Ghost and Spirit of truth are one and the same.
17:
reformed Gill takes the Spirit of truth to name the true Spirit of God, dictator of the Scriptures of truth, who leads men into the truths of the gospel and gives boldness to confess them before men. Calvin calls him the Master or Teacher of truth: until we are inwardly instructed by him, the understandings of all of us are seized with vanity and falsehood. grammatical-historical Barnes says he is so called because he would guide them into all truth and keep them from all error. Ellicott is more precise: the office is to bring truth home to the hearts of men, to carry it out of the material sphere into the moral, and to make it more than a collection of signs seen or heard — a living power in living men. Robertson calls it a most exquisite title, set against the spirit of error. wesleyan-arminian Wesley compresses the office to four verbs: he has, reveals, testifies and defends the truth as it is in Jesus. Clarke widens it: the gospel itself may be so called, for exposing falsity and teaching the knowledge of the true God. Lightfoot supplies the occasion: the whole world then lay in falsehood, the Gentiles under a spirit of delusion and the Jews under the imposture of traditions, so that such a Spirit was seasonable.

Why the world cannot receive him is the sharper question. Barnes takes the world for all entirely under the influence of the things of this world; such men walk by sight, so that what does not gratify the senses makes no impression, and since they cannot see the Spirit’s operations they judge all said of his influence delusion. Clarke names them by their appetites — the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eye, the pride of life — and says they admit no influence that cannot be an object of sense; God is found everywhere in the operation of his hands except in the perverted passions of men, and there alone they look for him. Wesley says it in a phrase: no spiritual senses, no internal eye to discern him. Ellicott states the principle rather than the symptom: the Spirit can be received only by those who have the spiritual faculty, and the unbelieving world has lost that perception. Robertson agrees the sinful world left to itself is helpless, lacking spiritual insight and spiritual knowledge, and notes that it failed to recognise Jesus and fails in the same way with the Spirit. Calvin reads the exclusion as a measure of the gift: the contrast shows the peculiar excellence of a grace God bestows on none but his elect. All that Scripture tells us of the Holy Spirit is regarded by earthly men as a dream, because, trusting their own reason, they despise heavenly illumination.

On the last clause the emphasis reverses. Robertson notes the pronoun stands first for contrast — ye know him, over against the world — because they have seen Jesus, who reveals the Father. He distinguishes the prepositions: the Spirit abides by your side, at home with you, not merely in the midst of you, and then in you, in your hearts. He also observes that the relative pronoun, though grammatically neuter, is rightly rendered whom, since a person and not a mere influence is promised. Ellicott prefers the better text, which reads the second verb as a present — and is in you — setting the disciples’ receptivity against the moral blindness of the world: they had strengthened their spiritual faculties under Christ’s teaching, had in part received the Spirit, and by that reception were prepared for the fuller gift. Clarke says the same: they had already received a measure of the truth. Wesley makes the indwelling permanent and domestic: he shall be in you as a constant guest, and your bodies and souls shall be temples of the Holy Ghost.
18:
grammatical-historical Ellicott calls the rendering comfortless unfortunate, since it suggests a link with Comforter which the Greek does not have; the margin’s orphans is exact, and the same translators render it fatherless at the only other place it occurs in the New Testament. Robertson notes it means bereft of parents and is common in the papyri, though since Christ had just called the disciples little children the sense may simply be helpless. wesleyan-arminian Clarke gives two derivations — one from a word for what is dark, since an orphan is left to wander in obscurity, one from a Hebrew root meaning to strip bare — and adds the custom behind the image: the disciples of a Hebrew teacher called him father, were called his children, and at his death were reckoned orphans. Wesley says only that the word is elegantly applied to those who have lost a friend.

reformed Gill takes Christ to stand as a father to his people, so that the disciples might well fear being left as children without a father. Among the latin-fathers, Augustine of Hippo makes the point with a scruple attached: it was not the Son who adopted sons to his Father, nor is that Father ours by nature as he is his, yet Christ displays paternal feelings here, as he elsewhere calls us children of the bridegroom. Augustine sets the promise against the gift just made, lest anyone think that because the Spirit was to be given Christ would not himself be present. puritan-evangelical Henry catches the tone of a parting: friends ask each other to write as often as they can, and this Christ engages — that out of sight they should not be out of mind. The departure was neither total nor final, and the case of true believers, though sometimes sorrowful, is never comfortless, because they are never orphans.

What the coming is divides them. Ellicott holds that the context shows it to be the spiritual presence in the person of the Paraclete. Henry reads the present tense as immediate — I do come — and refers it first to the resurrection. Clarke takes both: he would come again in rising from the dead, and after the ascension they would be made partakers of the Spirit, their comforter and guide for ever. Barnes strings the answers together: though he was to die he would live again, though absent in body he would be present by his Spirit, though he went to heaven he would return. Augustine warns that they are not to look for the same kind of presence over again: he will come, but not to live with them every day as before, and to them alone, so that what he had said to the Jews still stands.

Calvin turns the verse into a doctrine of dependence. It shows what men are when deprived of the Spirit’s protection: exposed to every kind of fraud and injustice, incapable of governing themselves, unable of themselves to do anything. The only remedy is that Christ govern us by his Spirit, and the disciples are first reminded of their weakness so that, distrusting themselves, they rely on nothing but his protection. The promise also settles a question of manner: in saying he will come, he shows how he dwells in his people and fills all things — by the power of his Spirit — so that the grace of the Spirit is a striking proof of his divinity. Hilary adds a further mode. Christ is in the Father by the nature of his divinity, and we are in him by his birth in the flesh; he in turn is to be believed in us by the mystery of the sacrament, as he testified that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood dwells in him and he in them.
19:
reformed Gill takes the first clause literally: the men of the world see Christ with their bodily eyes, which is all the sight they have, and in a very little while they will be deprived even of that, until he comes in the clouds, when every eye shall see him. grammatical-historical Barnes dates the saying to the day before the death and agrees the world would not see him visibly again until the judgment, having no eye of faith meanwhile. Robertson notes the emphatic pronoun that follows, set against the blind and unseeing world. Ellicott refers that seeing to the spiritual presence of the Paraclete, granting a first fulfilment in the appearances of the forty days but arguing that these were steps in an education leading from trust in a physical presence to trust in a spiritual one. To the world the grave seemed the closing scene; to those with power to see him he appeared as living, and was in very deed more truly with them and in them than before. Calvin says the same: we must not judge Christ’s presence or absence by carnal perception, but employ the eyes of faith to contemplate his power, so that believers always have him present by his Spirit and behold him though distant in body.

Ellicott prefers the reading for I live, and ye shall live, and takes the present tense strictly: it is the essential life of which Christ is the source, unaffected by the death he is about to pass through, and believers have that principle of life even here, developed into its fulness hereafter. Robertson calls the continued living of Jesus the guarantee of eternal life, the surety of a better covenant. wesleyan-arminian Clarke makes it a pledge twice over: as surely as he shall rise, so shall they; and because he lives a life of intercession at God’s right hand, they shall live a life of grace here and glory hereafter. Wesley divides it by the two natures — the living One in his divine nature, risen in his human nature — so that they live the life of faith on earth and afterwards the life of glory. Barnes denies the clause refers particularly to the resurrection: it points to Christ’s continuing to live, since he had a nature which could not die, and the Christian’s life depends on that. Calvin allows the clause to be read either as confirming what precedes or as standing alone, embraces the first, and draws the second from it anyway: the life of Christ is the cause of our life.

What is meant by that day spreads the witnesses across a span. Barnes and Clarke place it after the resurrection, when the risen Christ would make plain that he lived and they be convinced that he and the Father are one. Wesley takes it of the resurrection but more eminently of Pentecost; Robertson of the whole new dispensation of the Spirit. Ellicott names Pentecost as the first reference while holding the words equally true of every spiritual quickening and of the final coming. Calvin is broadest: it denotes the uninterrupted course of a single day, running from the moment Christ exerted the power of his Spirit to the last resurrection, so that the knowing began then, but feebly. Ellicott says they would no longer seek a manifestation from outside, as Philip had asked, but would read the Father in the life of Christ brought home to their hearts, and from the depth of their inmost lives cry Abba, Father. Calvin insists this union cannot be reached by indolent speculation, but only when Christ diffuses his life in us by the secret efficacy of the Spirit; and he sets aside an old misuse of the verse to prove Christ God only by participation, since the words speak not of his eternal essence merely but of the divine power manifested in him.
21:
The verse is read as a ladder. grammatical-historical Ellicott sets out the successive degrees leading up to the full manifestation of Christ: first the moral apprehension and practical observance of the commandments, which follow necessarily from love to him; then a special receptivity to the Father’s love, so that there is a particular sense in which the Father loves such a man — the words carrying full emphasis, he it is, and he only; and then the special love of the Son, accompanied by the manifestation. Robertson notes the same emphatic demonstrative in the Greek, that is the one who loves me, and adds that the unseen and risen Christ will be a real and spiritual presence to the obedient and loving believer.

Barnes reads the chain in the opposite direction, as evidence of a union already asserted. True love to Jesus produces obedience; those who love him are loved of the Father, which shows a union between Father and Son; and Jesus loves them too, which shows the same union again. From this he draws a wider conclusion: the love of one holy being is the love of all, the kingdom of God is one, and his people, though called by different names, are united to each other and to God by love. To manifest, he adds, is to place an object before the eyes so that it may be seen; Christ will so show himself to his followers that they shall see and know he is their Saviour.

reformed Gill will not let hath my commandments mean mere possession of a text: not the external revelation of them in the Bible only, but the commandments written on the heart by the finger of the Spirit, and kept under the influence of grace received from him. wesleyan-arminian Wesley says the same in five words — written in his heart — and glosses the manifestation as being made more abundantly. Clarke divides the promise in two: all the faithful disciples should see Christ after his resurrection, and he will manifest his power and goodness to all who believe and obey him, even to the end of the world.

Calvin explains why the test of love is repeated so often. There is nothing to which we are more prone than to slide into a carnal affection, so as to love something else than Christ under the name of Christ; to have the commandments is to be properly instructed in them, and to keep them is to conform our life to their rule. He then faces the difficulty the verse raises for the order of grace. Christ appears to speak as though men loved God before he loved them, which is absurd, since he reconciled us while we were enemies and we did not first love him. But no debate about cause and effect is being conducted here, and no inference can be drawn that our love comes first: the meaning is that all who love Christ will be happy because they have a testimony of the Father’s love engraved on their hearts, not that God then begins to love them. Knowledge, he grants, goes before love; yet Christ’s promise is that those who purely observe his doctrine will make progress from day to day in faith and approach him more nearly and familiarly. From this Calvin draws both an encouragement and a warning: the fruit of piety is progress in the knowledge of Christ, hypocrites are rejected, and the reason many fall back, so that scarcely one in ten proceeds in the right course, is that they do not deserve such a gift. A more abundant knowledge of Christ, held out here as the reward of loving him, is an invaluable treasure.
22:
reformed Gill identifies the speaker as Judas Lebbaeus, surnamed Thaddaeus, the same as Jude the apostle and author of the epistle bearing his name, the words not Iscariot added to distinguish him from the betrayer. Barnes and Clarke agree, both naming him the brother of James. grammatical-historical Ellicott says the phrase distinguishes him beyond all possibility of confusion from the man who had gone out into the darkness. Robertson makes the same point and adds a count: this is the fourth interruption of the discourse, after Peter, Thomas and Philip. Among the latin-fathers, Augustine contrasts the characters — not the traitor, but he whose epistle is read among the canonical Scriptures — and Augustine of Hippo sharpens it: Judas the holy, not the impure; the follower, not the persecutor.

What lay behind the question divides them. Ellicott holds that manifest raised in Judas the expectation see had raised in Philip — a visible manifestation like the one granted to Moses, such as was looked for at the Messiah’s advent. It ran contrary to every thought of the Messiah that it should be to a few only, since his reign was to be the judgment of the Gentiles and the establishing of the theocracy. The phrase rendered how is it, Ellicott notes, means literally what has happened that, so that Judas is wondering whether something has occurred to cause a departure from the expected course. Robertson reads it likewise as a suspicion of changed plan, and Clarke supposes Judas thought the kingdom must extend over all the earth. Barnes offers a plainer account: Judas probably took the promise of the resurrection only, and did not see how Christ could show himself to them without being seen by all.

Augustine takes the reply to answer the question directly. Christ manifests himself to his own and not to aliens because the one love him and the other do not; love is what distinguishes the saints from the world, making men of one mind in a house, and it is in that house that the Father and the Son take up their abode. There is an inner manifestation of God unknown to the ungodly, to whom the Father is not manifested at all and the Son only in the flesh — a showing for a little while and not for ever, for judgment and not for joy, for punishment and not for reward. Of the promise that they will come to him, Augustine observes that they come to us in that we go to them, and that they come by succouring.

Calvin thinks the question fair and the answer incomplete. Not without reason does Judas ask why Christ imparts his light to so few, since he is the sun of righteousness by whom the whole world ought to be enlightened. But the reply does not solve the whole question, saying nothing of the first cause. Christ finds all men at the outset alike, entirely alienated from him, so that he cannot choose someone who already loves him but chooses from among his enemies those whose hearts he bends to love him. He did not intend to raise that distinction here: his design was to exhort them to the earnest study of godliness, so he is content with the one mark separating them from the world, that they keep the doctrine of the gospel — a mark that follows the beginning of faith, being the effect of their calling. Augustine of Hippo, for his part, turns the exchange into a lesson in how to read: while the disciples question and Jesus replies, we too are learning alongside them whenever we read or hear the Gospel, and we should place ourselves among the questioners and listen to our common Master.
23:
grammatical-historical Ellicott takes the reply as a restatement of the condition that must hold on man’s side — and so as the answer to Judas: the world, in its unbelief and without the spirit of love, could not receive the manifestation. Robertson reads a continuing condition, if one keep on loving me, and calls it the key to the promise; the plural we will come is Father and Son together, not at the judgment but here and now. If the Spirit abides in a man, that heart becomes a temple fit for both.

Barnes fills in what the coming brings: pardon, peace of conscience and joy in the Holy Ghost, God manifesting himself as a Father and Jesus as a Saviour, religion being God returning to the soul and showing himself reconciled. Make our abode he takes as figurative and deliberately not temporary: they take up residence in the heart as a temple fit for their abode. wesleyan-arminian Clarke widens the opening clause past the men in the room to all who would believe through their word or their successors’, and the Father will call such a man his child and make his heart a temple where Father, Son and Spirit dwell to eternity. Ellicott adds that the thought was familiar, since the Old Testament had long spoken of God dwelling in a sanctuary among his people; and outside Scripture Philo urges that since God enters the soul invisibly we should prepare that place to be an abode worthy of him, or he will quit us unawares for one better provided.

Whether the Father’s love answers to ours, and in what order, divides them. Wesley states a proportion — the more a man loves and obeys, the more God will love him — and says the coming implies a manifestation of the divine presence beside which what is given in justification is as nothing. reformed Calvin resists that ordering. God’s love toward us is not placed in the second rank, as though it followed our piety as its cause; the verse assures believers that their obedience pleases God and that they may look for fresh gifts. Christ speaks not of the eternal love with which God loved us before the world was made, but of the point at which he seals it on our hearts by adoption, and not of the first illumination but of the degrees by which faith advances. From this Calvin refuses the inference, common in his day, that we love God naturally before regeneration and so merit the grace of it.

The negative half draws the same line from the other side. Ellicott says that having shown how Father and Son take up their abode in believers, Christ now shows how they could not be manifested to the world: he who does not love Christ does not keep his word, and that word is the Father’s; having rejected the love of God revealed in the Son he has closed the channels of communion himself, and God cannot dwell where there is nothing receptive of the divine presence. Robertson gives the participle its force: the one who keeps on not loving me. Gill divides the failure in two, applying it to outward professors who observe the ordinances without love and to the profane world which pays them no regard; he takes the whole as justifying Christ’s manifesting himself to his disciples and not to the world. Clarke draws the plainest conclusion: the man not obedient to Christ’s testimonies does not love him. Calvin turns it pastoral: believers are mixed with unbelievers and must be agitated by storms, so they are warned not to look at the world in such a way as to depend on it. To keep them from wavering at its obstinacy Christ secures credit for his doctrine by testifying that it is from God, not contrived by men on the earth.
25:
grammatical-historical Ellicott renders the first clause while abiding with you: he had been speaking words they found hard to understand, and now breaks off to tell them of the Spirit who would interpret them. Robertson notes the perfect tense, for permanent keeping. reformed Gill lists what these things covers: the Father, the Father’s house and the way to both, and the keeping of his commandments. Barnes adds that the Spirit would be given as their guide besides. puritan-evangelical Henry hears two things: that Christ does not retract what he has said, and that he had used his bodily presence to the utmost, losing no time; from which he draws a rule for hearers whose teachers are about to be removed.

Calvin reads the sentence as an antidote to despair. Christ says it lest they lose heart at having profited less than they ought, for he had scattered a seed of doctrine that lay hidden and as it were suffocated in them; they are to look for consolation in the doctrine already heard, and be of good courage until the Holy Spirit, the inward Teacher, speaks the same thing in their hearts. Calvin generalises: we grow weary of what is obscure, whereas we must be patient until the Spirit enables us to understand what we thought we had read or heard to no purpose. Among the latin-fathers, Augustine of Hippo distinguishes two dwellings. The one promised is spiritual, realised inwardly by the mind; the one now declared is bodily, exhibited outwardly to eye and ear. The first brings eternal blessedness to the delivered, the second visits in time those awaiting deliverance; as regards the first the Lord never withdraws, as regards the second he comes and goes.

On the promise the witnesses press the scope of all things. Barnes takes it of all the apostles needed for their office, including what they were not then prepared to hear, and as a full promise of inspiration covering the organising of the church and the recording of its truths; the bringing to remembrance he divides between a reminding of sayings otherwise forgotten and a presiding over their memories in composing the sacred history. wesleyan-arminian Clarke says the Spirit takes away every doubt, and that the recollection was exact enough for the apostles to transmit the identical words Jesus uttered. Wesley limits it to what was necessary for them to know, extending it to their successors so far as saving truth goes. Lightfoot draws the line hardest: it may be fitly asked whether any besides the apostles were ever taught all things, and his answer is that every believer is led into all truth necessary for himself, while the apostles alone were led into all truth necessary for the whole church. Ellicott finds the limit inside the verse, all things being bounded by whatsoever I have said unto you, and takes in my name to mean as Christ’s representative.

Robertson notes that the relative, though grammatically neuter, is rightly rendered whom, and that the Father sends the Spirit while the Son sends him too, with no contradiction in that relation of the persons; after Pentecost the disciples could recall and understand what Jesus had said. Gill weighs the title once more: the word means an advocate who pleads another’s cause before kings, which suits the Spirit promised to speak in the apostles before governors; yet since it also means comforter, which agrees with their condition, he judges that sense the more proper here. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem fastens on the second verb: Christ said not only that the Spirit would teach but that he would bring to remembrance whatever had been said, the teaching of Christ and of the Spirit being one. From the Spirit’s recorded speech — on the road toward Gaza, to the apostles at Antioch — he shows a Spirit living, calling and sending with authority.
27:
reformed Gill treats the words as a will: Christ, about to die, bequeaths the best legacy he has. wesleyan-arminian Clarke calls it his last and best dying legacy, and glosses not as the world giveth as the difference between salutations of custom and a wish its speaker can perform. grammatical-historical Ellicott, starting from the same ordinary greeting, notes that the emphatic my makes it an actual possession imparted. Robertson adds that the common greeting is raised here to a spiritual peace only Christ can give. Calvin places the difference in effect: men have the word coldly in their mouth, or wish it sincerely and cannot bestow it, whereas this peace comes with the thing itself. Wesley divides the clauses: peace with God and with our consciences, and the peace Christ himself enjoys and creates.

eastern-antiochene Chrysostom hears farewell and consolation together, love and fear being uppermost. latin-fathers Augustine of Hippo puts the fear concretely: their hearts might be troubled at his going, lest in the shepherd’s absence the wolf attack the flock. His answer is that as God he did not abandon those from whom he departed as man, going away in the nature subject to local limits and remaining in that which is everywhere, so that his quitting their sight left his presence in their heart untouched. Clarke gives the second verb its force: the heart is not to shrink back in fear. eastern-alexandrian Origen turns the gift into an image: a house meant to stand is built in fine weather, and so withstands the flood; the house of reason, which shelters the speculations of truth, must likewise be built while the soul is quiet and at peace.

On the reproof that follows, Barnes denies it means they had no love: they had low views of him and inherited prejudices, and this is a friend’s tender reproof. Robertson finds the same in the grammar. Ellicott states the principle: true love seeks another’s good, and their sorrow was at root selfish, as all sorrow is for those who depart to be with God. puritan-evangelical Henry says Christ gives another reason why their hearts should not be troubled, that his own was not, and that the leave taken at such a parting is a good night, not a farewell.

The closing clause is the most disputed in the chapter. Ellicott observes that it has been controverted in every age of the church, and rejects the common defence that the Father is greater only as regards the Son’s human nature; a subordination of the Son within the divine nature, he holds, is plainly asserted here. Robertson answers that the filial relation makes the comparison necessary, that it marks rank and not essence, and that the need to explain it proves the deity of the Son. Clarke takes the sender to be greater than the sent, and holds the saying easily reconciled with orthodoxy, since Christ speaks now of one nature and now of the other. Barnes shifts from nature to condition: rejoice that I leave this humiliation and resume my former glory. Hilary asks: if the Father is greater by giving, is the Son less by confessing the gift? The giver is greater, but he to whom unity with the giver is given is not the less. Calvin says the passage has been tortured various ways: the Arians used it to make Christ an inferior God, and the orthodox fathers replied that it must refer to his human nature — a reply he judges inappropriate. Christ speaks of neither nature here, but places himself between God and us: the words show not how he differs from the Father, but why he descended, to raise us where we could not reach. Chrysostom reads the encouragement as accommodation to their weakness: when you hear that I go to my Father you should rejoice, since I go to one able to change all things.
29:
reformed Gill takes the foretelling as proof of Christ’s deity, since none but the omniscient God can tell of things before they come to pass, which is what distinguishes him from the gods of the nations. grammatical-historical Barnes agrees the point is evidential: they were to be confirmed in faith by the power of foretelling events. wesleyan-arminian Clarke adds a pastoral motive: lest his death be a stumbling-block, he has spoken of it beforehand and shown its necessity, so that their sorrow might be mitigated. Ellicott says two readings are possible: that Christ foretold the coming of the Advocate so that its fulfilment might increase their faith, or that he foretold his going so that when the hour came they might believe he had gone; he prefers the first. Calvin treats the clause as a concession: since they cannot yet comprehend so deep a mystery he will bear with them until the event happens and interprets the doctrine. Though for a time he seemed to speak to the deaf, his words were not scattered in the air but were a seed thrown into the earth.

Among the latin-fathers, Augustine of Hippo objects: ought not a man to believe before the thing comes to pass? The very praise of faith is that what is believed is not seen — witness the reproof of the disciple who believed because he had seen, and the blessing on those who have not seen and yet believe. Faith is the assurance of things not seen; and he hardly knows whether anyone can be said to believe what he sees at all.

On the next verse Gill notes the limit: not much more before his death, though after the resurrection he talked with them over forty days; the point is to mark the departure near and quicken their attention. Calvin generalises: abundance takes away the appetite, and we delight more in what is soon taken from us; our own course being short, we ought to seize the present opportunity. He notes too that Christ speaks by circumlocution rather than saying plainly that he will soon die, lest a death so hideous make them faint, for to believe in him crucified is, on the face of it, to seek life in hell. Ellicott hears the discourse broken off by the thought that the hour of conflict is at hand, and takes the prince of evil to be working by Judas.

Robertson identifies him as Satan, and Ellicott insists the denial be taken absolutely: he possesses nothing in the person of Christ and has never for a moment ruled in him, from which it follows that the surrender of himself is entirely voluntary. Barnes explains the mechanism: temptation has power only because there are principles in us answering to the tempter’s designs, so where no such propensity exists it has no purchase; and he supposes much of the anguish in the garden came from conflict with that enemy. Wesley states three denials: no right, no claim, no power; no guilt to give him a hold, no corruption to side with his temptation. Lightfoot narrows the title: in the common acceptation of the Jewish nation it meant the devil ruling among the Gentiles, and the moment was almost come when Christ and the devil should contend for that dominion. Calvin guards the word: the devil is called prince not because he has a kingdom separate from God, but because by God’s permission he exercises tyranny over the world; and Christ goes away not under compulsion but in obedience to the Father. Clarke reports that many manuscripts and versions omit the word this, which he thinks makes the sense more general, and canvasses two further identifications: the ruler who is Christ himself at his return, and the Roman government which by its deputy would judge him.
31:
The sentence is hard to punctuate. grammatical-historical Ellicott judges it most probable that the stop after so I do be dropped and everything before it governed by that, giving one sentence. Robertson keeps the break and supplies an ellipsis, something like I surrendered myself to death, before the purpose clause. Calvin reports both and leaves the choice to the reader.

On what the obedience shows, Ellicott looks back to the prince of this world: he is coming, but to a defeat, and the very world he has ruled will see in this self-sacrifice the love of the Father, which will reclaim men from bondage into the freedom of children. reformed Gill narrows the term, taking the world to mean not the unbelieving world but the world of God’s elect. Barnes reads it as a demonstration under test: it was not to be alleged that Christ’s virtue had never been tried, and he passed through the severest temptations so that human nature might be seen capable of resisting them. wesleyan-arminian Wesley puts it in Christ’s own voice: I suffer him to assault me because it is the Father’s commission, to convince the world of my love in being obedient unto death. Calvin sets the decree of God above the scene, so that none may suppose Christ was dragged to death by the violence of Satan: God appointed his Son to be the propitiation, and permitted Satan for a short time to treat him with scorn as though he had won. Christ does not resist, in order to obey his Father and offer that obedience as the ransom of our righteousness.

eastern-antiochene John Chrysostom uses the summons to make a point about courage. Ignorance makes the soul timid, instruction in heavenly doctrines makes it great; fear is a matter of will, not of nature, since what is natural is immutable. The disciples were fearful before they had learned what they ought, and afterwards bolder than lions: Peter, who could not bear the threat of a servant girl, was later hung head downwards and scourged without falling silent. He raises the objection that Christ said arise, let us go hence for fear the plotters would seize him before his teaching was done, and dismisses it as beneath his dignity. Clarke draws a lesson: Christ goes to die as a sacrifice, out of love to mankind and with unshaken courage, and all our actions should be formed on that plan — the love of God and man their principle, his glory their end, his will their rule.

Where the rest of the discourse was spoken divides them most. Barnes reports it commonly supposed that Jesus and the apostles rose from the paschal supper and went toward the Mount of Olives, the following chapters and the prayer being delivered on the way to Gethsemane; others suppose they merely rose from the table. He prefers the former. Robertson agrees the group apparently walked out into the night, the rest being spoken in the shadows on the road. Clarke reports the same reconstruction from an earlier commentator, adding that it was near midnight, the moon almost full. Ellicott calls it a question that cannot be settled, noting that the connection between this verse and the opening of the next chapter suggests both were spoken in the same place. Lightfoot places the discourse earlier and elsewhere: at Bethany, on the very day of the passover, as they were about to walk to Jerusalem, the later chapters belonging to the evening after the supper. Wesley agrees, taking let us go hence to mean into the city, to the passover, and assigning the following chapters to the city, before he crossed the brook Kedron. Calvin knows the road theory but finds it more probable, given what is said afterwards about that crossing, that Christ was exhorting the disciples to the same obedience they had seen in him.
